reasons.C1: Unmonitorable vector channels are a real oversight gap; snapping as a cheap receiver-side control is a concrete, deployable countermeasure finding.
reasons.C2: Reproduced 10 of 10 checkpoints, proper null and shuffled-label controls; but channels non-adaptive, trained pre-sprint, no colluding agents.
reasons.C3: Figure 1 tells the story instantly, but 13 pages exceeds the 8-page limit and dilutes the core result.

levers.C1: Show snapping survives an adaptive channel trained against it, in an actual multi-agent collusion game rather than key-value recall.
levers.C2: Train channels adversarially against each countermeasure, publish checkpoints, and add significance tests across more seeds and a second task.
levers.C3: Cut to 8 pages: one problem paragraph, Figure 1, a single countermeasure table, limitations; move probes and length sweeps to appendix.

N6.verdict: Most evidenced entry; snapping kills the channel cleanly, but it is a carrier study and the attacker never fights back.

reasons.C1: Secret price-fixing offers to pricing agents is a relevant insider-threat framing, but builds on well-trodden LLM duopoly setups.
reasons.C2: Strong test discipline and preregistration, but zero real model runs; no results, no model chosen, configs are placeholders.
reasons.C3: Report not seen; only README and tests, so problem, method and findings cannot be read as a paper.

levers.C1: Show that trusted-partner framing changes behaviour versus direct offers, quantifying a social-engineering attack surface on pricing agents.
levers.C2: Run the 60 preregistered games on two real model families and report the positive control and Wilson intervals per condition.
levers.C3: Write the 8-page report with a single condition-by-acceptance table and the dual-use appendix.

W6.verdict: Clean harness and honest preregistration, but a test suite is not a result; without real runs there is nothing to judge.

reasons.C1: Self-funding detection via fund-flow hops is standard fraud and wash-trading practice; applying it to x402 agent markets is modest novelty.
reasons.C2: Held-out split, permutation test, bootstrap; but CI spans 0.56 to 1.00, labels share rule evidence, label-independent rule p = 0.14.
reasons.C3: Problem and results are legible, but 17 pages breaks the limit and the agent-collusion link stays implicit.

levers.C1: Demonstrate the flagged wallets are LLM agents and show the signal catches collusion missed by existing exchange-grade wash-trading heuristics.
levers.C2: Get independent labels from another team on many more families and test against adaptive rings that route through exchanges.
levers.C3: Cut to 8 pages and lead with one held-out results table plus the label-leakage caveat stated up front.

R6.verdict: Practical ledger forensics I would want in production, but circular labels and unverified agents keep it off the collusion question.

reasons.C1: Testing whether leniency and fines act on LLM agents as on humans is policy-relevant and goes beyond existing LLM-collusion replications.
reasons.C2: No code exists; plan is sound with contamination tests and preregistration, but four regimes solo in 48 hours is tight.
reasons.C3: Clear question, one-table demo and explicit cut order; nothing written yet beyond the plan.

levers.C1: Deliver the human-versus-LLM scorecard showing at least one regime that works on people but fails on agents, with intervals.
levers.C2: Ship the harness validated against the paper's tables, the laissez-faire positive control, and all four regimes with per-duopole seeds.
levers.C3: Produce the 8-page report around the four-column regime table with contamination results and the dual-use appendix.

F8.verdict: Best question in the room and a credible plan, but until the positive control runs it is a proposal, not evidence.
